content: The potential advantages and disadvantages of different lighting conditions in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) for preterm and low birth weight infants have not been clearly quantified. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of cycled light (CL), defined as approximately 12 hours of light followed by 12 hours of darkness, on the growth of preterm infants at three and six months' corrected age (CA). It also sought to compare the effects of CL with irregularly dimmed light (DL) or near darkness (ND), as well as with continuous bright light (CBL), on growth outcomes at the same time points. Subgroup analyses were conducted to assess the impact of introducing CL at different postmenstrual ages (PMAs)—before 32 weeks, at 32 weeks, and from 36 weeks PMA—and to compare its effects on small-for-gestational-age infants versus appropriately grown infants. The researchers used the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group's standard search strategy to identify relevant studies. They searched multiple databases, including CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL, up to January 2016. They also reviewed clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and reference lists of retrieved articles. Only randomized or quasi-randomized trials comparing CL with ND or CBL in preterm and low birth weight infants were included. Data collection and analysis followed Cochrane methods, and the quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. A total of nine studies involving 544 infants were included in the analysis, with one additional study added in this update. The overall quality of the studies was low, primarily due to small sample sizes and lack of blinding. Six studies (424 infants) compared CL with ND. None of these studies reported weight outcomes at three or six months. One study (40 infants) found no significant difference in weight at four months between the CL and ND groups. Another study (62 infants) showed that the day-night activity ratio before discharge was higher in the CL group, indicating 18% more daytime activity compared to the ND group. Two studies (189 infants) assessed the incidence of severe retinopathy of prematurity (stage ≥ 3) and found no significant differences between the CL and ND groups. Two studies (77 infants) reported a significantly shorter hospital stay in the CL group compared to the ND group, with a weighted mean difference (WMD) of 13 days. The quality of evidence for this outcome was rated as low. One study (37 infants) found that infants in the CL group cried less at 11 weeks' corrected age compared to the ND group. Three studies (120 infants) compared CL with CBL. Two studies (79 infants) reported a significantly shorter hospital stay in the CL group compared to the CBL group, with a WMD of 16.5 days. The quality of evidence for this outcome was also rated as low. One study (41 infants) found that infants in the CL group had a higher mean weight at three months' corrected age and spent fewer hours awake in a 24-hour period at three months. Another study (41 infants) reported a shorter duration of ventilator use in the CL group compared to the CBL group, with a mean difference of 18.2 days. Additionally, one study (41 infants) found that the time to first oral feeding was shorter in the CL group by 6.8 days. No safety concerns were identified in any of the studies. In conclusion, trials evaluating the effects of CL have included 544 infants, but none reported on the primary outcome of weight at three or six months. The findings suggest that CL, compared to both ND and CBL, may reduce the length of hospital stay. However, the quality of evidence for these outcomes is low. Future research should prioritize comparing CL with ND to better understand its potential benefits and risks.
